newsitem.title: CROATIA: UN confirms 60 executed by Serbs were patients.
newsitem.headline: UN confirms 60 executed by Serbs were patients.

text.p: U.N. war-crimes investigators have identified 60 of about 200 bodies exhumed from a mass grave in eastern Croatia and confirmed they were hospital patients executed by Serb forces in 1991, state media said on Thursday.

The state news agency HINA quoted Croatia's deputy prime minister, Ivica Kostovic, as saying the remaining bodies would be identified by Croatian experts. Final identification would be made with the help of next-of-kin.

U.N. experts working for the Hague-based International Criminal Tribunal on former Yugoslavia (ICTY) confirmed the victims were patients who had minor injuries and were taken from the hospital in the town of Vukovar by besieging Serb troops.
They were later executed in the vicinity of the Ovcara grave, a few km (miles) south of the town, HINA said.

Vukovar, on the Danube River border with Serbia, was demolished in a ferocious three-month siege by Yugoslav army regulars backing a local Serb minority revolt against Croatia's declaration of independence from federal Yugoslavia.
Earlier autopsies showed all Ovcara victims died of multiple gunshot wounds consistent with an execution-style killing, rather than wounds that would have been incurred in battle.
The bodies were all male, ranging from teenagers to men in their 60s, and none was found in military uniform.
The Hague tribunal has indicted three Yugoslav army officers for war crimes and crimes against humanity in connection with the Ovcara killings, but all are still free, apparently in Yugoslavia.
Kostovic told HINA that the ICTY now hadf enough evidence to bolster the Ovcara-related indictments.
ICTY investigators working with the U.S.-based Physicians for Human Rights group completed exhumations last autumn.
Eastern Slavonia is the last Serb-held enclave in Croatia, due to revert to government rule later this year after a transitional period under U.N. administration.
